meta.title: Honest VIETNAM Guide 2026: The ONLY Video You Need To Watch
meta.description:
This is the Vietnam guide for people who’ve already watched five videos that all say the same thing.

By the end, you’ll know how long to actually spend, whether Halong Bay is worth booking (and what to do instead if it isn’t), the itinerary mistakes that turn a trip into a blur of overnight buses, and the parts of the country — Ha Giang, Phong Nha, the war history — that most guides skip entirely.

⏱️ CHAPTERS
01:43 — Understanding the Place
05:26 — When to Go & Seasonal Reality
08:44 — Getting There & Getting Around
12:51 — How Long & How Much
16:40 — Where to Stay & Base Yourself
19:23 — What to Do (Beyond the Obvious)
29:16 — Food, Drink & Local Life
35:06 — Honest Truths
43:14 — Practical Planning Summary


🗺️ TRIP PLANNING RESOURCES

✈️ Flights
Fly into Hanoi and out of Ho Chi Minh City (or the reverse) rather than doubling back — it's the only way to see the full length of the country without retracing your steps.
▶ Compare routes and prices here: https://www.skyscanner.net
▶ Book directly with Vietnam Airlines here: https://www.vietnamairlines.com

🏨 Accommodation
Where you base yourself changes the trip more than most guides admit — Tây Hồ over the Old Quarter in Hanoi, An Bang Beach over the ancient town in Hội An, a guesthouse that actually knows the roads in Ha Giang.
▶ Plan your stay here: https://www.booking.com
▶ For dorms and hostel-based travel: https://www.hostelworld.com
▶ For local guesthouses and homestays — often the better option in smaller towns like Ha Giang and Phong Nha, where hotel chains don't reach: https://www.airbnb.com

🚗 Getting Around
▶ Grab is the one app you'll open every day — taxis, bikes and food, in every city this film covers: https://www.grab.com/vn/en/
▶ For the overnight sleeper train between Hanoi, Huế and Đà Nẵng, book the soft sleeper ahead of time — Vietnam Railways' own site doesn't take foreign cards: https://www.baolau.com/en/transportation/vietnam/trains/

🎟️ Experiences & Activities
▶ Browse experiences here for Halong Bay and Lan Ha Bay cruises, and Ha Giang Loop Easy Rider tours: https://www.klook.com
▶ Sơn Đoòng — the cave at the centre of the Phong Nha section — has exactly one licensed operator. Details and availability here: https://oxalisadventure.com — Expeditions now book up to a year ahead.
▶ For comparing prices and reviews on day tours — Cu Chi Tunnels, Mekong Delta, cooking classes: https://www.getyourguide.com and https://www.viator.com

🧭 Essential Information
▶ Many UK, EU and other nationalities now get 45 days visa-free. Everyone else can apply online for a 90-day e-visa. Apply only through the official portal — convincing lookalikes exist: https://evisa.gov.vn

Current official travel advice:
▶ US State Department — https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/traveladvisories/traveladvisories/vietnam-travel-advisory.html
▶ UK FCDO — https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/vietnam

📱 Useful Tools & Apps
▶ An eSIM gets you connected the moment you land, on the country's strongest network: https://www.airalo.com/vietnam-esim
▶ Prefer a physical SIM? Viettel counters are in every arrivals hall: https://vietteltelecom.vn/en

🛡️ Before You Go
▶ If you're riding a motorbike, check your policy actually covers it before you go. This one does, up to 125cc with a valid licence: https://www.worldnomads.com/travel-insurance/destinations/vietnam

Emergency numbers in Vietnam: Police 113 · Fire 114 · Ambulance 115

If this helped you plan your own trip — or if there's something we missed — let us know in the comments.

🌍 If this destination helped you decide, this one might too:
▶ JAPAN Travel Guide 2026 — https://youtu.be/DBCm9hzUSzw

⚠️ Note: Travel information changes over time. Prices, visa requirements, entry rules, accommodation taxes, transport passes, opening hours, and local regulations can change after publication. Always verify the latest practical details through official sources before travelling.

📘 Join the Honest Planet Facebook page: https://www.facebook.com/HonestPlanet
A place for honest travel stories beyond the videos: what places really feel like, what they cost, the mistakes people make, and the details most guides leave out, from destinations around the world.

transcript: If you’re trying to figure  out how to travel Vietnam,   or if you’ve already lost a weekend to  Vietnam research and noticed every video   covers the same five places, the same  six dishes, and the same thirty-second   scam warning that never actually tells  you what to do — this one is different. We went through hundreds of real travellers’  experiences — the mistakes people made,   the money they lost, the questions that never  got a straight answer — and built the guide   those videos should have been. By the end, you  won’t just know what Vietnam looks like. You’ll   know exactly how to do it properly, and whether  the parts that matter to you are actually there. The most common mistake people make when planning  a trip to Vietnam is deciding to see all of it. Vietnam is 1,650 kilometres long. Narrower  than England, but stretching further than   the distance from London to Athens. And the  standard itinerary — two weeks, north to south,   hitting every highlight — sounds reasonable  until you’re on your fourth overnight bus in   ten days, arriving somewhere new and  exhausted. Seeing everything through   a fog of transit. Never quite landing  anywhere long enough to understand it. The people who come back from Vietnam  talking about how it changed them are   almost never the ones who did the  two-week sprint. They’re the ones   who slowed down. Who stayed four nights  somewhere they’d only planned two. Who   missed Hoi An because they got stuck in Phong  Nha and couldn’t bring themselves to leave. Understanding why that matters,  before you book anything,   is the difference between a trip you  remember and a trip you survived. This guide is built around that understanding. From the northern border with China to the  southernmost tip of the Mekong Delta, Vietnam   is longer than California and narrower than most  people’s mental image of a country — an elongated   S-shape pressed between mountains and sea, with  a coastline running almost its entire length. This geography is not just a geography lesson. It   is the single most important piece  of information for planning a trip.   Vietnam is, in practice, three different  countries sharing one name and one passport stamp. The North — centred on Hanoi — is older, more  formal, more layered with history. The streets   are narrower and the pace is different. The  food is different. The relationship to the   war and to the country’s past is more present  in the daily texture of life. The north is also   where Vietnam’s most extraordinary landscapes  exist: the limestone mountains of Ha Giang along   the Chinese border, the karst formations of  Ninh Binh rising from flooded rice fields,   and the karst bay of Ha Long, where the  same limestone geology meets the sea. The Centre is the country’s emotional and  historical core. Hue was Vietnam’s imperial   capital — a city of palaces, citadels, and a  melancholy that doesn’t feel affected. Hoi An is a   preserved trading port so beautiful it has become  the most visited town in the country, with all   the complications that brings. Between them, the  Hai Van Pass traces the coast, and further west,   the cave systems of Phong Nha sit among the  most dramatic natural environments on earth. The South runs at a different speed. Ho Chi  Minh City — what most of its residents still   call Saigon — is relentless economic energy. More  international, more open, and chaotic in a way   that feels less considered than the north. Beyond  the city, the Mekong Delta spreads across the flat   southern plain in a web of waterways and floating  markets — flat, green, waterlogged, built around   the river rather than roads. It rewards slow  travel more than almost anywhere else in Vietnam. These three regions don’t just look  different. They feel different,   eat different, and suit different  kinds of travellers. The north   rewards patience and physical curiosity.  The centre rewards slow mornings and an   interest in history. The south rewards  openness and a tolerance for noise. One more dimension cuts across all three:  Vietnam is a deeply spiritual country in   ways that aren’t always visible to a visitor in  a hurry. The incense burning at roadside shrines,   the early morning pagoda visits, the ancestor  altars in the back rooms of restaurants — this   is not heritage tourism. It is how the  country organises its relationship with   the past and the present simultaneously. You  see it everywhere once you remember to look. Vietnam is not dangerous — currently the same  safety tier as most of Western Europe according   to the US State Department, with low crime  against tourists. What it does require is a   working understanding of how it operates: which  taxis to take, which cruise operators to trust,   how the currency works, how to cross a road  without freezing at the kerb. Those specific   pieces of knowledge are what separate  arriving defensive from leaving changed. The most misleading answer you’ll  find about Vietnam is “the best   time to visit.” Most guides answer it  with a month or a season. The honest   answer is that Vietnam has three simultaneous  climate systems running across its length,   and the best time depends entirely on  which part of the country you’re going to. The North — Hanoi, Ha Giang, Sapa, Ninh Binh  — is best from October through April. Autumn   brings clear skies and cooler temperatures. Winter  — December through February — is genuinely cold by   Southeast Asia standards. Hanoi sits at 12 to  16°C in January. Sapa, at elevation, can drop   below freezing. If you’re packing based on the  assumption that Southeast Asia means warm, you   will arrive underprepared. Spring, from March into  early May, gives warmth, colour, and some of the   best road conditions in the north. The exception  worth knowing: September into October, just before   the dry season properly begins, is when the rice  terraces of the far north — Ha Giang, Sapa, Mu   Cang Chai — are at their most extraordinary. The  harvest colours the hillsides in gradients of gold   and green that the dry season months don’t offer.  Mountain roads in the far north can close after   heavy rain even in the dry months — worth building  a day’s flexibility into any Ha Giang itinerary. Central Vietnam — Hue, Da Nang, Hoi An —  operates on an almost opposite calendar.   The dry season runs from February through  August. From October through December,   central Vietnam is in its peak rainy  season, and in bad years that means   genuine flooding in Hoi An’s ancient  town. This is the single most common   mismatch between expectation and reality.  Travellers arrive in November expecting the   Southeast Asia they saw in photographs  and find a grey, waterlogged landscape. The South — Ho Chi Minh City, the Mekong,   Con Dao — is best from November  through April. Outside that window,   it’s hot and humid, with afternoon rains that  arrive reliably and clear. Mornings still work. The nationwide sweet spot — if you’re doing  north to south in a single trip — is March   to early May. The north is warm, the centre is  dry, and the south is past its wettest months. Tet — the Vietnamese Lunar New Year, falling  in late January or February — operates by its   own rules entirely. Transport prices  surge dramatically. Domestic flights   sell out months in advance. Much of  Hanoi shuts for the better part of a   week. If you want to experience  Tet, base yourself in the south   or with a Vietnamese family. If you want  to sightsee productively, plan around it. Vietnam is easier to reach now than most  existing guides will tell you. Vietnam   Airlines added thirteen new international routes  in 2025, including direct connections from Milan,   Copenhagen, Delhi, and Mumbai.  Hanoi’s Noi Bai Airport expanded   its international terminal in December  2025, raising capacity by fifty percent. For most Western travellers, the realistic entry  points are Hanoi in the north and Ho Chi Minh City   in the south. Flying into one and out of the other  — the open-jaw approach — is structurally the most   sensible way to experience the full length  of the country without retracing your steps. One planning note for late 2026 onward: the new  Long Thanh international airport — 50 kilometres   from central Ho Chi Minh City — has had  its ceremonial opening and is targeting   full commercial operations from late 2026.  If you’re booking travel for 2027 or beyond,   verify which airport your  airline is actually using. Once you’re in, the country’s  scale reasserts itself — and   so does the need for a transport strategy. For city transport: use Grab. Always.  Street-hailed taxis carry a scam risk   that Grab simply removes — it sets the  fare before you move, tracks the route,   and eliminates the primary scam vector  for city transport in one step. To use   Grab from the moment you land, buy a Viettel  SIM from the official counter in arrivals:   around $10 to $15 US dollars for a month  of data with the best rural coverage in the   country. An eSIM purchased before departure  does the same job without the airport queue. For travel between major cities: domestic  flights are cheaper than most people expect.   Vietjet and Bamboo Airways regularly  offer those routes for well under   fifty US dollars when booked in advance —  sometimes as low as twenty — often barely   more expensive than an overnight bus,  and removing a fifteen-hour journey. One thing worth knowing for domestic  flights: Vietnamese budget carriers — Vietjet   especially — do weigh carry-on bags at the gate,  and enforce limits more strictly than travellers   used to European or American low-cost  airlines expect. If you’re planning to   travel carry-on only, check the specific  allowance before you fly and pack to it. For overnight ground travel: the Reunification  Express train is worth knowing. Book a soft   sleeper — a four-berth cabin. Vietnam Railways’  website doesn’t reliably accept foreign payment   methods — Baolau and 12go Asia handle this  cleanly for a small commission. Book one   to two weeks ahead on popular routes. The train  earns its place when the journey is part of the   trip — the coastal stretch between Da Nang and Hue  is one of the great rail routes in Southeast Asia. VIP sleeper buses are the ground alternative:   a semi-private pod with a reclining bed, USB  charging, and functional air conditioning,   for around eight to ten dollars more than a  standard seat. Worth knowing: overnight buses   carry a road risk the train eliminates. For long  overnight journeys, the train is the safer option. One change worth knowing for Hanoi visitors:  authorities have introduced restrictions on   gas-powered motorbikes in parts of the  historic centre — currently applying   to a small area on weekend evenings, with  broader restrictions still in discussion.   It’s worth checking the current status before  you visit, as the policy is still evolving. How long you need depends entirely on what   you’re trying to do — and most first-time  planners dramatically underestimate both. Ten days is enough for one region, done properly.  That means either the north — Hanoi, Ninh Binh,   maybe Ha Giang if you have four of those  days free — or the south — Ho Chi Minh City,   the Mekong Delta, and Con Dao if you’re willing to  add a short flight. Ten days trying to cover both   ends of a 1,650-kilometre country means spending  more time in transit than in any single location. Fourteen days — the most common trip  length — works for two regions connected   by a domestic flight. You arrive in  each place having actually rested,   rather than disoriented from an overnight journey. Three weeks or more is what the full  north-to-south route actually requires.   Ha Giang alone needs four to five days  minimum. The Mekong Delta needs two to   three nights — the floating markets run from  early morning and are largely done by nine;   a day trip from Ho Chi Minh City arrives  too late to see them properly. These   aren’t add-ons. They’re the experiences  that define what Vietnam actually is. For context on local prices: twenty-six thousand  dong is roughly one US dollar. Throughout   this guide, pre-trip costs are given in US  dollars. On-the-ground prices appear in dong,   with approximate dollar conversions  shown on screen, based on current rates. A quick word on the numbers themselves —  because the dong’s denominations trip up   almost every first-time visitor. Notes run  from 1,000 up to 500,000, and doing mental   arithmetic under pressure at a market stall is  genuinely difficult at first. A useful shortcut:   treat anything under 10,000 dong — the 1,000,  2,000, and 5,000 notes — as loose change,   the equivalent of coins. They won’t buy you  much on their own. The notes that matter are the   20,000 upward. Once that distinction clicks, the  mental conversion becomes significantly easier. Budget, in real terms: street food meals typically  run 40,000 to 80,000 dong. A dorm bed in a good   hostel costs around 160,000 to 240,000 dong. A  Grab ride across central Hanoi is about 40,000   dong. A street corner bia hoi — draught  beer — is as little as 8,000 dong in Hanoi. Ultra-budget travellers — dorms, street food, no  tours — can manage 520,000 to 920,000 dong per   day. Mid-range — private rooms, occasional  restaurant meals, local tours — runs from   1,300,000 to 2,400,000. Three or four-star hotels  push that toward 3,200,000 dong. Comfortable   travel with nicer accommodation and organised  experiences runs from 3,200,000 dong upward. These figures cover accommodation, food,  and local transport. Organised tours sit   on top — and tourist-zone inflation is  real, particularly for Halong Bay cruises   and peak-season accommodation in Hoi An. Vietnam  remains extraordinary value by Western standards.   But visitor numbers surpassed 21,000,000 in  2025 — twenty percent above the pre-pandemic   peak — and prices have followed. Arrive with  2018 expectations and you’ll be surprised. Vietnam is a country you move through rather than  settle in — most stays are two to four nights,   then onward. But where you base yourself in each  city shapes the trip more than most guides admit. In Hanoi, the Old Quarter is the obvious  choice for first-timers and delivers on   the chaos and character — streets named for  the goods once traded there, French colonial   buildings in various states of preservation,  the lake at the heart of the quarter catching   light differently at every hour. The trade-off  is noise and accommodation that tends to be small   and vertical. Some motorbike restrictions have  been introduced in parts of the historic centre,   though the Old Quarter remains busy — the  density and tourist pricing are unchanged.   For a quieter base with better-value  food, the Tay Ho district around West   Lake is worth considering — it has become  the base of choice for longer-stay visitors,   which means the café infrastructure and  liveability are a cut above the Old Quarter. In Hoi An, the accommodation question matters  enormously. The ancient town has limited hotel   options and heavy tourist pricing. Staying  near An Bang Beach — a fifteen-minute cycle   away — puts you close to a working fishing  community at significantly better value,   with the old town reachable by  bicycle. In peak season — December   through February — accommodation fills  up weeks or months ahead. Book early. In Ho Chi Minh City, District 1 is central and  prices itself accordingly. Districts 3 and Binh   Thanh offer better value and genuine neighbourhood  character without the tourist-strip pricing. In Hue, the area south of the Perfume River  — the main hotel and restaurant district,   with the citadel a short bridge-crossing  away — is the most practical base,   and accommodation here is significantly  cheaper than equivalent quality in Hoi   An. Hue rewards at least two full days —  the Imperial Citadel alone is a half-day,   and the Thien Mu Pagoda, the royal tombs, and the  Demilitarised Zone to the north each add depth.   It is a city that reveals itself slowly,  which is the correct speed for it. For Ha Giang and Phong Nha: book ahead. These are  not large towns, accommodation fills during peak   months, and the right guesthouse — one whose staff  know road conditions, can arrange an Easy Rider,   and can point you to where locals eat — makes  a significant difference to the experience. Halong Bay. It’s where every  Vietnam conversation starts. The UNESCO World Heritage Site. The limestone  karsts rising from emerald water. The image that   appears on every Vietnam guide, poster, and travel  magazine from the past thirty years. It is real,   and it is genuinely spectacular — thousands of  islands and islets scattered across the bay,   formed from limestone eroded  over millions of years. Here is what the drone footage doesn’t show you:   eight hundred boats operating in the bay  simultaneously. Six hundred overnight   cruise ships during peak season. In the  core areas closest to the main harbour,   the experience can feel less like a natural  wonder and more like a floating hotel corridor. None of this means you shouldn’t go. Water  quality data from 2025 showed measurable   improvement across the bay, even as the  core tourist corridors remain among the   most trafficked waters in Southeast Asia.  It just means you need a decision framework. Under one hundred US dollars for an overnight  cruise is a documented gamble: poor food,   overcrowded decks, nothing like the photographs.  The realistic entry point for a genuinely good   experience is $130 to $180 US dollars — booked  through your hostel or directly through a   verified platform, not from street-front offices  in Hanoi’s Old Quarter claiming large discounts.   $200 and above buys meaningful differences  in food quality, cabin size, and itinerary. But there are better alternatives  for most travellers. Lan Ha Bay,   accessed from Cat Ba Island just  south of the main Ha Long Bay zone,   has the same geology with a fraction of the  boat traffic, cleaner water, and kayaking   through caves that feel genuinely remote. Bai  Tu Long Bay, to the northeast, receives even   fewer visitors — the default recommendation  for travellers who want to skip the crowded   core entirely. For most visitors, these aren’t  compromises. They’re often the better choice. For the karst landscape without the sea:  Ninh Binh, two hours south of Hanoi,   is where limestone formations  rise from flooded rice paddies.   Boat trips through caves and gorges at Trang  An deliver a quieter, more meditative version   of the same visual drama — without seasickness,  without the crowds, and with the added dimension   of ancient temples and a landscape that  has been farmed and lived in for centuries. If Ninh Binh is the Halong alternative most people   stumble onto eventually, Ha Giang is the  place most people never reach at all. Ha Giang is in the far north, on the Chinese  border, and requires time and intention to   reach. The Loop — a roughly three to four  hundred-kilometre circuit of mountain roads   through Hmong and Tay minority villages — is  described by almost everyone who has ridden it   in language usually reserved for defining life  experiences. Four to five days minimum through   a limestone landscape of extraordinary  drama: passes that disappear into clouds,   valleys that drop a thousand metres below the  road, villages where no one speaks English and   tourist infrastructure is essentially absent. The  Ma Pi Leng Pass, along the Nho Que River gorge,   is frequently described as the single  most beautiful stretch of road in Vietnam. Ha Giang roads are genuinely dangerous  for inexperienced riders. The solution   is the Easy Rider format: you ride pillion  with a local guide who knows every corner.   One hundred thirty to one hundred eighty US  dollars for three to four days, inclusive of   accommodation and food. That’s not a compromise  — it’s the correct approach for most visitors,   and it means your attention goes to  the landscape rather than the road. Sapa offers a more accessible version of highland  Vietnam — rice terraces, minority villages,   and established trekking infrastructure. It  suits shorter itineraries and travellers who   want the highland experience without Ha Giang’s  time commitment. More developed and more visited,   which is either reassuring or limiting  depending on what you’re looking for. Heading south through the centre,  most itineraries skip the province   that contains the most extraordinary  natural environment in the country. Phong Nha, in Quang Binh province — midway between  Hue and Hanoi, with direct flights to Dong Hoi   airport — is the most consistent regret in nearly  every post-trip account from people who didn’t go.   It is home to Son Doong Cave: so  vast it has its own weather system   and forest floor inside it. A four-day  expedition through Oxalis Adventure — the   only licensed operator — costs around $3,000  with a limited number of permits per season.   Everyone who has done it says the same  thing: there is nothing else like it. For travellers not ready for Son Doong  Cave: Paradise Cave and Phong Nha Cave   are accessible without premium cost and genuinely  spectacular. The village itself — with its river,   its cycling routes, and its complete absence  of the tourist machinery that defines Hoi   An — is described by almost everyone  who stays as a place they left too soon. Hoi An deserves honest treatment, because it is  genuinely extraordinary and genuinely overrun in   equal measure. In the first half of 2025 alone,  Hoi An received nearly three million visitors. Here is what is still true:  Hoi An at six in the morning,   before the tour buses arrive, is one  of the most beautiful places in Asia.   That version of Hoi An still exists —  only for the people who wake up for it. The culinary reason to visit is real and specific:  Cao Lau is a noodle dish whose character,   locals say, comes partly from the water of  specific ancient wells in the city. White   Rose Dumplings are a Hoi An original. Mi  Quang is a turmeric-inflected noodle dish   that doesn’t exist with the same character  anywhere else. These dishes are Hoi An’s   contribution to the cuisine of a country  that takes regional specificity seriously. Hoi An has been a centre for custom tailoring for  centuries — you choose a fabric, bring a reference   photo or describe what you want, and have clothing  made to measure, usually within a few days.   The tailor shops are genuinely worthwhile —  but only with the right approach. Allow two   to three fittings over three to five days, not  same-day turnaround. Agree on price, fabric,   and style before anything is cut. Check stitching  before you pay the balance. Managed correctly,   it’s one of the great specific pleasures the  town offers. The results vary more than the   reputation suggests — the ceiling is genuinely  high, and so is the floor. Know that going in. Con Dao sits around an hour by plane from Ho  Chi Minh City and exists in almost complete   contrast to everything the mainland offers. It  was Vietnam’s most notorious prison island under   both French colonial and American-backed rule  — the Con Dao Prison complex is still there,   and understanding what happened inside it  changes how the landscape feels. That history   coexists with a national park covering  most of the island, near-empty beaches,   and some of the strongest diving in the  country. It suits travellers who want   a beach component but find Phu Quoc too developed. Ho Chi Minh City rewards one specific piece  of orientation that most guides omit: Cholon,   the city’s Chinese quarter in District 5, is  where the city’s Chinese-Vietnamese community   has traded and lived for over two centuries. The  Binh Tay Market operates on a scale that makes Ben   Thanh look like a gift shop. The temples, the  pharmacies, the dried goods shops running off   into side streets — Cholon is the part of Ho Chi  Minh City that doesn’t feel like it’s performing   for anyone. Worth an afternoon, and worth  getting there by Grab rather than a tour bus. The Mekong Delta is the experience most visitors  get wrong — usually by doing it as a day trip from   Ho Chi Minh City. The floating markets run from  before dawn and are largely finished by nine;   a tour bus from the city arrives two hours too  late and sees the shell of what was there. Two   nights in Can Tho or Vinh Long — where you can  hire a small boat at five in the morning and   be out on the water before anyone else — is  an entirely different experience. Flat, slow,   waterlogged, built on a rhythm the city  doesn’t share. It is one of the genuinely   distinct ways Vietnam surprises people who  thought they knew what they were coming for. Vietnamese cuisine is not one thing.  This is the most important piece of   information that every “best food in  Vietnam” list fails to communicate.   The north, the centre, and the south eat  differently — not as variations on a theme,   but as genuinely distinct culinary traditions with  their own ingredients, their own flavour profiles,   and their own dishes that barely exist  outside the region that created them. I am up before six. The pho shop near my house has  been open since before midnight — the broth has   been going that long, and the people on those  small stools, leaning over their bowls in the   morning cold — they are not tourists. They  are teachers. Drivers. People going to work. Pho in the north is not the same thing you  find in the south. My broth — the broth I   grew up with — is clear, built slowly from  bone, deep without being heavy. You eat it   with your eyes first. The white noodles, the thin  slices of beef, the herbs you add yourself at the   table. There is no recipe for how long you  sit there afterward. That part is up to you. Bun cha is from here too — charcoal-grilled pork,   the patties and the belly, with a sweet-vinegar  broth and rice noodles and herbs. You dip,   you don’t mix. It’s a lunch dish. You won’t find  it done the same way anywhere south of here. And then there is egg coffee — ca phe trung. It   was invented in this city during  a time when fresh milk was scarce,   and what began as a solution became something  better than what it replaced. Whipped egg yolk,   strong Vietnamese drip — something between  a drink and a dessert. You eat it slowly.   Usually upstairs somewhere, looking out over a  street that has no interest in waiting for you. The café, in Hanoi, is not somewhere you go to be  efficient. It is somewhere you go to exist for a   while. A plastic stool, a drip filter over  a glass, the sound of the street. For less   than a dollar — that is what this city gives  you. And it is one of the best things it has. Bun bo Hue — I don’t talk about  it quietly. It is my city’s dish,   and most of the world hasn’t found it  yet. Honestly, I’m a little proud of that. The broth takes hours. Lemongrass, shrimp  paste, slow heat. It is spicier than pho,   richer, more complex — a bowl that asks  something of you and gives back more.   I eat it in the morning, at a small place  near the river, the steam rising in the cool   Hue air. There is no correct way to visit  this city without eating it at least twice. Hue has carried a lot of history, and you feel  that in the pace here — slower than Hanoi,   more reflective. The food is the same way. It  doesn’t announce itself. It rewards attention. Saigon moves fast, and the food moves with it. Banh mi here is not sandwich. The bread  is lighter than in the north — crispier,   almost delicate — and what goes inside is its own  world: pâté, cold cuts, pickled daikon and carrot,   fresh coriander, sliced chilli, a little  mayonnaise if you want it. It costs almost   nothing, and it is one of the great street  foods on earth. I say this without modesty. Com tam — broken rice — that is what the city  eats for lunch. The rice cracks during milling   and would have been thrown away once.  Now it is the base for grilled pork,   a fried egg, pickled vegetables,  small bowl of broth on the side.   The best versions are always at places with no  sign out front and a line of motorbikes outside. Coconut coffee came from here.  Vietnamese drip over coconut   cream and ice — cold and rich and sweet  in a way that makes sense only in this   heat. You drink it slowly. Even in  Saigon, some things resist the pace. For eating well anywhere in Vietnam: follow  the locals. A small place with simple,   plastic stools, no English menu,  and people sitting close together is   almost always a good sign. Busy and simple  means the food is fresh and moves quickly. One practical note before we leave food behind.  Your body may take a day or two to adjust — new   ingredients, new bacteria, a different pace of  eating. Most travellers never have a problem. The   ones who do are usually the ones who ignored  the basics: choose busy stalls where food is   moving fast and cooked to order, drink bottled  or filtered water, and treat ice outside major   cities with some caution. That’s it. Vietnamese  street food culture is built on freshness and high   turnover. The anxiety most first-timers arrive  with dissolves, usually, by the second morning. In the United States and most Western countries,  it’s called the Vietnam War. In Vietnam,   it’s called the American War. That  difference is not a translation issue.   It is the entire gap between the version  of history taught in Western schools and   the version of history that three million  Vietnamese people are still living with   in their bodies — right now — because of the  multi-generational effects of Agent Orange. The war ended in 1975. That is within  living memory of many Vietnamese people,   and within the lifetimes of their parents  for almost everyone currently working   in the country’s tourism industry. Agent  Orange doesn’t only affect the generation   that was exposed. An estimated three million  Vietnamese people live with its effects today. I don’t explain the museum to visitors before  they go in. There is no explanation that would   prepare you, and I have learned  that the ones who understand it   best are the ones who walk through  it without being told how to feel. What I can tell you is this: the people in  those photographs are not history to me. They   are grandparents. They are the reason certain  families here are smaller than they should be,   or carry conditions that cannot be fully  explained, or light incense at altars for   people who should still be alive. The war ended  fifty years ago. Its consequences did not. When you come out, the city will feel exactly  the same as when you went in — the noise,   the motorbikes, the smell of street  food and exhaust. And something will be   different anyway. That is the correct  response. That feeling is accurate. American travellers specifically  often express anxiety about how   they’ll be received. The honest answer is:  warmly. Most Vietnamese under forty do not   lead with the war in conversation.  The country’s economic energy is   genuinely forward-looking. The warmth that  travellers consistently report is real,   and it coexists — in the same people —  with a history that hasn’t fully closed. What this means for a visitor: you cannot  fully understand what you’re experiencing in   Vietnam without engaging with this history.  The Cu Chi Tunnels outside Ho Chi Minh City   are not an adventure playground — they are  a survival system used by people defending   their land. The Reunification Palace  is where the war ended — specifically,   on the morning of April 30, 1975, when a  North Vietnamese tank drove through its gates.   The palace is largely unchanged — the war room,  the command centre, the rooftop where the flag   was raised. Walking into it with that knowledge is  a different experience from walking in without it. Separately — and with considerably less weight —  the scam question. Three situations carry genuine   risk. The first is the airport taxi at Hanoi’s Noi  Bai airport— use Grab before you leave arrivals.   The second is Halong Bay cruise  booking through unvetted operators:   book through your hostel or a verified  platform, not from street-front offices   in Hanoi’s Old Quarter claiming large discounts.  The third is currency confusion — the 500,000 and   20,000 dong notes are similar in colour and have  been deliberately switched by dishonest vendors.   Count change immediately and  visibly, every single time. That’s it. Three situations, three  specific solutions. The people who get   caught are the people who didn’t know  the mechanics in advance. Now you do. On solo female travel: Vietnam consistently  rates as one of the safest destinations in   Southeast Asia for women travelling alone.  Grab eliminates the primary harassment   vector. A well-reviewed hostel, rather than an  isolated guesthouse — particularly outside major   cities — is worth factoring into accommodation  decisions. Violent crime against tourists is   very low. For all travellers, bag snatching  from passing motorbikes is a real risk — wear   bags across the body, carry cameras by the  wrist strap, and walk away from the kerb. For LGBTQ+ travellers: Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh  City have visible and welcoming urban scenes,   and personal safety in both cities is generally  good. Public displays of affection draw attention   regardless of orientation — Vietnam is  socially conservative in public spaces.   Legal protections are absent, and rural  areas operate on more traditional norms. Worth naming plainly: Vietnam is a  one-party state, and press freedom   and political expression are significantly  restricted. This is context for an informed   traveller — not a day-to-day safety concern,  but worth understanding before you go. On motorbikes: a valid Vietnamese driver’s licence  is technically required even with an international   permit — enforcement is inconsistent, but it  affects your insurance position if you have an   accident. If you have no motorbike experience,  Vietnam is not the place to start, and the Ha   Giang roads specifically are not forgiving.  Travel policies that exclude motorbike riding   are common; an accident without valid cover  in Vietnam is a serious financial situation. Travel insurance that explicitly  covers medical evacuation is worth   having — international hospitals in Hanoi  and Ho Chi Minh City are well-equipped,   but costs are paid upfront and English-speaking  care outside the main cities is limited. One thing no one tells you before you  arrive, and everyone figures out on day one:   crossing the road. Vietnamese traffic doesn’t  stop for pedestrians. It flows around them.   And it freezes tourists — sometimes literally  — on the kerb. You’ll see them standing there,   waiting for a gap that isn’t coming, while the  city moves around them and the minutes pass. What you do instead is step off the kerb at  a steady, predictable pace and keep walking.   The motorbikes read you and move around you.  That’s the system. It works because everyone   in it understands it. The moment you hesitate —  or panic and speed up — you become unpredictable,   and unpredictable is the only thing  that actually causes problems. Steady pace. Don’t stop. Don’t rush. And if there’s a Vietnamese  person standing next to you   at the kerb — watch them. When they go,  go with them. That’s the entire lesson. Vietnam has beaches, but it is not a beach  destination in the way that Thailand’s   Andaman Coast or the Philippines are. The  most developed coastlines — Nha Trang,   Da Nang — are heavily built up. Phu Quoc has  developed fast enough that the infrastructure   is still catching up. If you’re coming to Vietnam  primarily for beaches, that expectation deserves   honest examination. If you’re coming  for mountains, cities, caves, history,   and food — with beaches as a bonus — Vietnam will  exceed almost every expectation you arrive with. The travellers who arrive expecting beaches  often leave wishing they’d spent that   week in Ha Giang instead. That pattern is  consistent enough to name before you plan. Here is what you need before you book anything. When to go: The nationwide sweet spot is  March to early May. For the north only,   October through April works well. Be cautious  about central Vietnam from October through   December — peak rainy season, and in bad years  that means real flooding in Hoi An. Around   Tet — late January or February — expect transport  prices to surge and domestic flights to sell out. How long: Ten days for one region done properly.  Fourteen days for two, connected by a domestic   flight. Three weeks or more for the full country  without the sensation of always being in transit. Getting there: Fly into Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City.  The open-jaw approach — in one, out the other —   saves retracing your steps. If booking into Ho  Chi Minh City, verify which airport your airline   is using — Long Thanh International Airport is  coming online and the transition is underway. Getting around: Grab for all city transport.  Domestic flights for long hauls — book in advance.   Baolau or 12go Asia for train bookings. Easy  Rider for Ha Giang if you don’t have motorbike   experience. In parts of Hanoi’s historic centre,  motorbike restrictions now apply on weekend   evenings — check the current status before  you visit, as the policy is still evolving. Daily budget: Twenty to thirty-five US dollars  on a backpacker budget. Fifty to ninety for   mid-range. The main cost outliers: an Easy  Rider in Ha Giang runs one hundred thirty to   one hundred eighty US dollars for three to four  days inclusive; a mid-range Halong Bay cruise   starts at a similar figure; Son Doong Cave is in  a different category at three thousand dollars. Visas: UK citizens and citizens of most EU  countries — including Germany, France, Italy,   Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands, Poland, and  others added in 2025 — now have forty-five-day   visa-free entry. Most other nationalities  can apply online for a ninety-day e-visa at   twenty-five US dollars for single entry,  fifty for multiple entry. Always verify   against official Vietnamese government  sources before booking — rules change. Health and insurance: Get travel  insurance that explicitly covers   motorbike riding if you intend to ride  — many standard policies exclude it.   Cover for medical evacuation  is worth the additional cost. SIM card: Viettel from the official airport  counter — not from touts. Best rural coverage,   including Ha Giang and Sapa. Ten to fourteen US  dollars for a month of data. An eSIM purchased   before departure gives you connectivity  — and Grab — from the moment you land. Money: ATM fees here are higher than  almost anywhere else in Southeast Asia,   and the combination of your home bank’s  international charge plus the local ATM fee   can run to $15 US dollars per transaction  — on withdrawals that some machines cap   at the equivalent of $85. Which, at Vietnam  prices, is two days of accommodation, meals,   and Grab rides. Gone in fees. And then you’re  back at the machine doing it again. TP Bank,   VP Bank, and VIB charge lower local fees than  most, but the smarter move is to arrive with   a reasonable amount of US dollars or euros  in clean, undamaged notes and exchange at a   gold shop on arrival — the jewellery exchange  counters found on most main streets. You’ll   get a better rate, pay no fees, and avoid the  queue entirely. Always count change immediately.   Keep banknotes in good condition — torn or  written-on notes will be refused at exchange. Don’t miss: Ha Giang, even if it means extending  your trip. The War Remnants Museum in Ho Chi Minh   City — especially because it will be heavy.  Ninh Binh or Lan Ha Bay as alternatives to,   or alongside, Halong Bay. Hoi  An before six in the morning.   Phong Nha — it is the most regretted  omission in nearly every post-trip account. Watch out for: Booking a Halong Bay cruise  under one hundred US dollars. Arriving in   central Vietnam between October  and December without checking the   forecast. And the two-week north-to-south  itinerary — the most damaging piece of   Vietnam travel advice in circulation,  consistently producing the same result:   exhaustion, transit, and the sensation of having  ticked boxes without understanding anything. What stays with people is  rarely what they planned for. It is the particular silence after the  War Remnants Museum — walking back out   into the noise of Ho Chi Minh City and  finding that everything looks slightly   different. Not worse. Just different. Like  a lens has shifted and won’t shift back. It is standing at the Ma Pi Leng Pass  at dawn, looking across a gorge so deep   and so still that the only sound is  wind, understanding — in the specific,   physical way you can only understand something  when you are standing inside it — that you   almost didn’t come here. That you nearly did  the two-week sprint and missed this entirely. It is a bowl of bun bo Hue at seven in the  morning at a place with no English menu and   four plastic stools, with construction workers  on one side and a woman reading the news on her   phone on the other, and the broth tasting  like something that took all night to make,   because it did. And the realisation,  somewhere in the middle of it, that   you’ve stopped waiting for Vietnam to feel  manageable — and started just being in it. These are not the experiences the standard guide   was built to find. They are the ones  that exist on the other side of it. Vietnam is not what the fearful version  of it assumes it is. It is a country   that requires a specific kind of attention —  patient, curious, willing to slow down — and   returns that attention with something that is  genuinely hard to name and harder to forget. The people who come back talking about  how it changed them are not the ones   who saw the most places. They are the ones  who stayed long enough to understand one.
